title: World Bank model places Tunisia third among selected cement exporters for CBAM trade exposure
period: 2022 trade and 2017-benchmarked emissions; CBAM definitive regime from 2026

rootCauses.cause: In the World Bank model, cement trade exposure depends jointly on the difference between Tunisia's sector-average carbon-cost intensity and the EU average, and Tunisia's cement-export dependence on the EU; the model does not identify firm-level emissions or realized liabilities.

indicators.name: Tunisia position among ten countries shown in World Bank cement Trade Exposure Index chart
Cement trade exposure index, World Bank model (2022 trade inputs)

projection.scenario: EU CBAM definitive regime; the cited World Bank estimate is a static full-phase-in exposure calculation using historical inputs, not a forecast of Tunisian firm payments in 2026
projection.method: World Bank Trade Exposure Index, using 2022 WITS mirror trade and emissions intensities benchmarked to 2017, with a notional USD 100 per metric ton CO2 certificate price

stakeholders: Ministry of Industry Mines and Energy
dataGaps: The estimate uses country-sector average emissions benchmarked to 2017 and 2022 mirror trade; it is not firm-specific, does not account for subsequent production changes, and is sensitive to the carbon-price assumption. Domestic carbon-price credits can lower incremental obligations.
Actual Tunisian cement exports to the EU, firm-level embedded emissions, and realized CBAM costs after the definitive regime begins are not established by these sources.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content: The World Bank’s model ranks Tunisia third in the cement chart and gives a trade exposure index of 6.59099% in its companion workbook. Its two inputs are how much of Tunisia’s cement exports go to the EU and how the modelled sector-average carbon payment compares with the EU average. The index is not a realised tax bill (SRC-TG-292, SRC-TG-296).

sections.heading: Root causes
sections.content:
The modelled exposure reflects both relative carbon-cost intensity against average EU production
and the value/share of cement exports directed to the EU. These are determinants within the
World Bank index, not a finding that individual Tunisian plants have the same emissions intensity or
that exporters themselves legally surrender CBAM certificates. The source warns that firm-level
emissions may differ from country-sector averages, domestic carbon prices may be credited, and
results vary with the carbon-price assumption (SRC-TG-292).

sections.heading: Evidence
sections.content: CBAM_RP.xlsx, worksheet fig1, row 14 gives Tunisia 6.59099%, rank 3 and an EU share of world cement exports of 65.4924%. The ACER reproduction rounds the same estimate to 6.59% (SRC-TG-296, SRC-TG-293). The graphic in the methodological note reports the ranking; the underlying workbook supplies numeric precision (SRC-TG-292).

sections.heading: Why confidence is what it is
sections.content: The published reproducibility workbook establishes the model output. Firm-level costs, realised liabilities and changes since the input years cannot be inferred from this index (SRC-TG-296).

sections.heading: Links to other sectors
sections.content:
CBAM is an EU trade and climate policy affecting cement, an energy-intensive industrial subsector.
FND-TG-290 addresses Tunisia's broader industrial energy use and audit information.

sections.heading: Verification
sections.content: The original World Bank results workbook confirms the cement trade exposure index (6.59099%, rank 3). ACER’s rounded 6.59% agrees (SRC-TG-296, SRC-TG-293). Neither is a realised cost to Tunisian firms.

resolvedSources.title: Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) Exposure Indices, Methodological Note (Prosperity Insight, June 2025)
resolvedSources.publisher: World Bank (M. Maliszewska, C. Fischer, E. Jung) and Purdue University (M. Chepeliev)
resolvedSources.extracts:
Note p. 1 (PDF p. 8), definition:

> A trade partner's exposure to the EU CBAM depends on two key factors: competitiveness loss, measured by carbon cost intensity relative to that of an average EU producer, and trade and economic dependence on the EU in affected sectors. Excess carbon payments are computed by valuing the differences in emission intensity between exporting countries and the EU for the relevant product exports to the EU at prevailing carbon prices.

Note p. 2 (PDF p. 9):

> 1. Trade Exposure Index (TEI) —excess carbon payments in proportion to the value of exports in a specific CBAM sector;

> This note presents key findings using World Bank WITS mirror trade data from 2022 and emission intensity data from Chepeliev et al. (2025) and Chepeliev and Corong (2022) benchmarked to 2017.

> Several countries display high values on the Trade Exposure Index (TEI) in CBAM-affected sectors: Mozambique in aluminum (7 percent), Belarus in cement (27 percent), Egypt in fertilizer (19 percent), and India in iron and steel (13 percent).

> Overall trade exposure to EU CBAM is expected to be limited. [...] Developing economies' economic exposure to CBAM is expected to be small. [...] Other countries have exposures below 0.1 percent.

Note p. 6 (PDF p. 13), carbon price assumption:

> In this paper, the notional value of CBAM certificates is set at USD100 per metric ton CO2, which is in the range of recent European Union Allowance (EUA) futures trading. The indices are proportional to the value of the price of EU ETS allowances; all indices would be twice (half) as large if the emissions price was twice (half) as large.

Note p. 11 (PDF p. 18), Figure 1, cement panels (rendered page read):

> Cement, panel b, countries ranked by excess carbon payments (% of cement exports to world): Belarus | Ukraine | Tunisia | Albania | Malaysia | Türkiye | Algeria | Serbia | Morocco | Brazil

> Cement, panel a: TUN plotted above the "EU average" band, inside the "Average of the three most carbon intesive EU countries" band; x-axis "Exports of cement to EU (% of exports of cement to world)"

English gloss: in the cement Trade Exposure Index chart, Tunisia ranks third of the ten countries
shown, after Belarus and Ukraine. Its carbon payment per dollar is above the EU average and in the
range of the three most carbon-intensive EU countries, and a large share of its cement exports
goes to the EU. Tunisia does not appear among the ten countries shown in the fertilizer panels.
Exact Tunisian values are not printed and are not read off the bars.

Note p. 12 (PDF p. 19), Figure 2 "CBAM Aggregate Trade Exposure Index (10 countries with the highest exposure)":

> Egypt, Arab Rep. | Uzbekistan | Ukraine | India | Mozambique | Nigeria | Kazakhstan | China | Tunisia | South Africa

Note p. 15 (PDF p. 22), Figure 4 "CBAM Economic Exposure Index (10 countries with the highest exposure)":

> Mozambique | Ukraine | Egypt, Arab Rep. | India | Uzbekistan | Kazakhstan | South Africa | Georgia | Tunisia | Indonesia

English gloss: Tunisia is ninth in the aggregate trade exposure ranking and ninth in the economic
exposure ranking; the note states that countries outside the top three have economic exposure
below 0.1% of GDP.
resolvedSources.notes:
Static exposure estimate, not a forecast: it values 2022 trade flows with 2017-benchmarked
country-average emission intensities at a notional USD 100/t CO2, assuming full phase-in. The
authors warn that firm-level emissions may differ from country averages and that domestic carbon
prices paid can be credited. Tunisian values are shown only graphically.

resolvedSources.title: Trade exposure index for selected countries and the CBAM sectors (%) (CHEST data item 1241)
resolvedSources.publisher: European Union Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators (ACER), based on World Bank Group and OECD
resolvedSources.extracts:
Data item header and source line:

> Trade exposure index for selected countries and the CBAM sectors (%)

> ACER based on World Bank Group and OECD policy brief: What to expect from the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism?, 2025.

Table row:

> Cement | Tunisia | 6.59

English gloss: ACER reproduces a trade exposure index of 6.59% for Tunisian cement, taken from a
2025 World Bank Group and OECD policy brief. The page shows "Last updated 2026-06-11".
resolvedSources.notes:
Secondary reproduction. The page does not define the index; it is presumably the World Bank
Trade Exposure Index (excess carbon payments as a share of sectoral exports, SRC-TG-292), but the
underlying World Bank/OECD brief was not opened, so its carbon price and data year are not
confirmed. The page is rendered by script and was read through WebFetch, not a raw download.

resolvedSources.title: Regulation (EU) 2023/956 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 10 May 2023 establishing a carbon border adjustment mechanism
resolvedSources.publisher: Official Journal of the European Union (EUR-Lex)
resolvedSources.extracts:
Recital on phase-in:

> To ensure a gradual transition from the current system of free allowances to the CBAM, the CBAM should be progressively phased in while free allowances in sectors covered by the CBAM are phased out.

Recital on declarations:

> The first CBAM declaration, in respect of the calendar year 2026, should be submitted by 31 May 2027.

Article 22(1), surrender of certificates:

> By 31 May of each year, and for the first time in 2027 for the year 2026, the authorised CBAM declarant shall surrender via the CBAM registry a number of CBAM certificates that corresponds to the embedded emissions declared [...] for the calendar year preceding the surrender.

Final article, application:

> Article 2(2) and Articles 4, 6 to 9, 15 and 19, Article 20(1), (3), (4) and (5), Articles 21 to 27 and 31 shall apply from 1 January 2026.

English gloss: CBAM's financial obligations apply from 1 January 2026; certificates for 2026
imports are surrendered for the first time by 31 May 2027; CBAM is phased in as free EU ETS
allowances in covered sectors are phased out.
resolvedSources.notes:
Original 2023 text as served by EUR-Lex at access. Later simplification amendments (2025) may
have changed declaration and surrender dates; the amending act was not opened. The yearly
phase-out schedule of free allocation (Article 31 and the ETS Directive) was not extracted. The
European Commission CBAM page (https://taxation-customs.ec.europa.eu/carbon-border-adjustment-mechanism_en)
states "As of 1 January 2026, CBAM is applicable under its definitive regime" and names the
covered sectors as "cement, iron and steel, aluminium, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen"
(read through WebFetch).

resolvedSources.title: Reproducibility package for CBAM Exposure Indices – Methodological Note
resolvedSources.extracts:
Workbook CBAM_RP.xlsx, fig1, row 14, product, country, trade exposure index (%) and rank:

> Cement | Tunisia | 6.590991973876953 | 3

Column F gives EU exports as 65.492424% of worldwide cement exports. The trade exposure index is a modelled relative carbon-payment measure; it is not a tariff, an invoice, or a percentage of national GDP. The sector-output indicator in fig3 is a separate measure.
